rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن جريج وأبو صالح
rows.claim: Most commentators, including Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, and Abu Salih, identify “the truth” here as God, exalted is He.
rows.anchor: هنا هو الله سبحانه وتعالى قاله الأكثرون، منهم مجاهد وابن جريج وأبو صالح

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas supplies the implied Arabic sense: “if the possessor of truth followed” their desires.
rows.anchor: وتقديره في العربية: ولو اتبع صاحب الحق قاله النحاس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One gloss takes “following” metaphorically as truth agreeing with their desires: if they could disbelieve and disobey without punishment through divine incapacity or ignorance, the heavens and earth would be corrupted.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: هو مجاز، أي لو وافق الحق أهواءهم فجعل موافقته اتباعا مجازا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says that if the truth were their claim that God has partners, the gods would disagree in their aims, disrupting governance and corrupting the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى ولو كان الحق ما يقولون من اتخاذ آلهة مع الله تعالى لتنافت الآلهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading says the world’s order would fail if truth followed human cravings, since desires differ and conflict; truth is to be followed and people must submit to it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «لو اتبع الحق أهواءهم» أي بما يهواه الناس ويشتهونه لبطل نظام العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view takes “the truth” as the Qur’an: if it had been revealed according to what they liked, the heavens and earth would be corrupted.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «الحق» القرآن أي لو نزل القرآن بما يحبون لفسدت السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi says “whoever is in them” refers to rational beings: the angels in the heavens and humans and jinn on earth.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى من يعقل من ملائكة السموات وإنس الأرض وجنها الماوردي

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud’s recitation reads “and what is between them”; al-Kalbi likewise understands the phrase to include creatures between heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: يعني وما بينهما من خلق وهي قراءة ابن مسعود «لفسدت السموات والأرض وما بينهما»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Kalbi’s explanation and Ibn Masud’s reading, corruption includes rational and nonrational beings, animals, and inanimate things.
rows.anchor: فيكون على تأويل الكلبي وقراءة ابن مسعود محمولا على فساد من يعقل وما لا يعقل من حيوان وجماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority reading’s apparent sense concerns rational creatures, since what lacks reason follows rational beings in their soundness or corruption.
rows.anchor: وظاهر التنزيل في قراءة الجمهور يكون محمولا على فساد ما يعقل من الحيوان لأن ما لا يعقل تابع لما يعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angel corruption would mean treating as lords those who are themselves governed, and worshipping beings who are themselves servants.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا ما يكون من الفساد يعود على من في السموات من الملائكة بأن جعلت أربابا وهي مربوبة، وعبدت وهي مستعبدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human corruption takes two forms: following desire, which is ruinous, and worshipping other than God, which is unbelief.
rows.anchor: وفساد الإنس يكون على وجهين: أحدهما: باتباع الهوى، وذلك مهلك. الثاني: بعبادة غير الله، وذلك كفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Corruption of the rest of creation is consequential, because it is governed by rational beings and their corruption reaches what they manage.
rows.anchor: وأما فساد ما عدا ذلك فيكون على وجه التبع لأنهم مدبرون بذوي العقول فعاد فساد المدبرين عليهم

rows.speaker: السدي وسفيان
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Sufyan explain “their reminder” as what brings them honor and prestige.
rows.anchor: أي بما فيه شرفهم وعزهم قاله السدي وسفيان

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains it as what contains mention of their reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: أي بما لهم فيه ذكر ثوابهم وعقابهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas understands it as clarification of the truth and of the religious matters they need.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: أي ببيان الحق وذكر ما لهم به حاجة من أمر الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite receiving this reminder, they turn away from it.
rows.anchor: فهم عن ذكرهم معرضون

rows.speaker: الحسن وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and others take the question to mean: do you ask them for payment for what you have brought them?
rows.anchor: أي أجرا على ما جئتهم به قاله الحسن وغيره

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي والأعمش ويحيى بن وثاب وابن عامر وأبو حيوة
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, al-Aʿmash, and Yahya b. Waththab read the first word with an alif; the others without. All read the second with an alif except Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Haywa, who omit it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي والأعمش ويحيى بن وثاب «خراجا» بألف. الباقون بغير ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sense is: are you asking them for provision? Your Lord’s provision is better.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أم تسألهم رزقا فرزق ربك خير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one can provide sustenance or bestow favor as God does.
rows.anchor: أي ليس يقدر أحد أن يرزق مثل رزقه، ولا ينعم مثل إنعامه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan also says God’s reward for obedience and calling people to Him is better than worldly gain; Quraysh offered to make the Prophet their richest man, but he did not accept.
rows.anchor: وقد عرضوا عليك أموالهم حتى تكون كأعين رجل من قريش فلم تجبهم إلى ذلك قال معناه الحسن

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says kharj and kharaj have the same meaning, though varying the wording is more elegant.
rows.anchor: والخرج والخراج واحد، إلا أن اختلاف الكلام أحسن قاله الأخفش

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim distinguishes kharj as a payment or fee and kharaj as a grant.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حاتم: الخرج الجعل، والخراج العطاء

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says kharj is the verbal noun, while kharaj is the noun.
rows.anchor: المبرد: الخرج المصدر، والخراج الاسم

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlaʾ distinguishes kharaj as what is owed from kharj as what one gives voluntarily.
rows.anchor: فقال: الخراج ما لزمك، والخرج ما تبرعت به

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: Another distinction attributed to Abu ʿAmr is that kharj is income from persons and kharaj income from land; al-Thaʿlabi and al-Mawardi transmit the two distinctions respectively.
rows.anchor: وعنه أن الخرج من الرقاب، والخراج من الأرض. ذكر الأول الثعلبي والثاني الماوردي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path is the upright religion.
rows.anchor: أي إلى دين قويم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word sirat means a road; religion is called a road because it leads to Paradise.
rows.anchor: والصراط في اللغة الطريق فسمي الدين طريقا لأنه يؤدي إلى الجنة فهو طريق إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here believing in the Hereafter means believing in resurrection.
rows.anchor: أي بالبعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation takes their deviation from the path as the same path already mentioned.
rows.anchor: قيل: هو مثل الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says they veer away from the road to Paradise until they arrive at the Fire.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم عن طريق الجنة لناكبون حتى يصيروا إلى النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nakaba means to turn aside from a road toward another; a nakba wind deviates from its course, and the worst wind is the crosswind called nakbaʾ.
rows.anchor: نكب عن الطريق ينكب نكوبا إذا عدل عنه ومال إلى غيره ومنه نكبت الريح إذا لم تستقم على مجرى

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة وأبو عمرو وعاصم والكوفيون وابن مسعود والحسن
rows.claim: Medinan readers, Abu ʿAmr, and ʿAsim read shaqwatuna; the Kufans except ʿAsim read shaqawatuna, also reported from Ibn Masʿud and al-Hasan.
rows.anchor: أبي عمرو وعاصم «شقوتنا» وقرأ الكوفيون إلا عاصما «شقاوتنا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words shaqāʾ and shaqā are also used, respectively with a long or short vowel.
rows.anchor: ويقال: شقاء وشقا بالمد والقصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best explanation is that their pleasures and desires overcame them; they are called misery because they lead to it.
rows.anchor: وأحسن ما قيل في معناه: غلبت علينا لذاتنا وأهواؤنا فسمى اللذات والأهواء شقوة، لأنهما يؤديان إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an similarly names the punishment that follows an act by the consequence already contained in it: consuming orphans’ wealth unjustly is described as eating fire.
rows.anchor: كما قال الله عز وجل: إن الذين يأكلون أموال اليتامى ظلما إنما يأكلون في بطونهم نارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says their misery was what God had foreknown and written for them in the Mother of the Book.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ما سبق في علمك، وكتب علينا في أم الكتاب من الشقاوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation is that they thought well of themselves and badly of other people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حسن الظن بالنفس وسوء الظن بالخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They confess that their actions had led them away from guidance.
rows.anchor: أي كنا في فعلنا ضالين عن الهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is a confession, not an excuse; their subsequent plea to leave Hell and promise not to return to wrongdoing supports that reading.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا اعتذار منهم إنما هو إقرار. ويدل على ذلك قولهم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmr reports that Hell’s inhabitants call Malik for forty years without reply; he eventually answers that they will remain there.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة يذكره عن أبي أيوب عن عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص قال

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
rows.claim: In Ibn ʿAmr’s report, they then call on God, are left unanswered for twice the span of the world, and are told to be driven away; afterward they speak no words, making only the sounds of donkeys—first an exhalation, then an inhalation.
rows.anchor: قال: ثم يدعون ربهم فيقولون:

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhi also transmits a similar account as a Prophetic report from Abu al-Dardaʾ.
rows.anchor: خرجه الترمذي مرفوعا بمعناه من حديث أبي الدرداء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada compares the disbelievers’ voices in Hell to a donkey’s bray, beginning with an exhalation and ending with an inhalation.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: صوت الكفار في النار كصوت الحمار، أوله زفير وآخره شهيق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the people of Hell will make barking sounds like dogs.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: يصير لهم نباح كنباح الكلاب

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muhammad b. Kaʿb al-Qurazi begins a report he says he heard about the people of Hell crying to the keepers; al-Qurtubi notes the full account in his al-Tadhkira.
rows.anchor: محمد بن كعب القرظي: بلغني أو ذكر لي أن أهل النار استغاثوا بالخزنة

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: In Muhammad b. Kaʿb’s account, after God reminds them that they had denied His signs, they expect mercy and repeat their plea; they interpret their “misery” as the decree written for them.
rows.anchor: ألم تكن آياتي تتلى عليكم فكنتم بها تكذبون

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: The report says God tells them to be driven away and speak no more; their supplication and hope cease, they bark at one another, and Hell is shut over them.
rows.anchor: فانقطع عند ذلك الدعاء والرجاء، وأقبل بعضهم على بعض ينبح بعضهم في وجوه بعض، وأطبقت عليهم

rows.speaker: حسان بن ثابت
rows.claim: The quoted poem praises ʿAʾisha as chaste, discreet, and above slander, of noble lineage and good character, purified by God, and vows the poet would never raise a hand to repeat the accusation; he pledges lifelong support for the Prophet’s family and says her rank exceeds challengers.
rows.anchor: حصان رزان ما تزن بريبة وتصبح غرثى من لحوم الغوافل حليلة خير الناس دينا ومنصبا

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report says that when Hassan recited “chaste and discreet,” ʿAʾisha replied that he was not so, implying he had fallen into slander; al-Qurtubi notes the contradiction.
rows.anchor: وقد روي أنه لما أنشدها: حصان رزان قالت له: لست كذلك تريد أنك وقعت في الغوافل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi reconciles the contradiction by suggesting Hassan did not state the accusation explicitly but alluded to it, so the remark was attributed to him.
rows.anchor: ويكون عرض بذلك وأومأ إليه فنسب ذلك إليه والله أعلم

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق وغيره
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq and others report that the Prophet punished two men and a woman for the slander: Mistah, Hassan, and Hamna; al-Tirmidhi also mentions this report.
rows.anchor: فروى محمد بن إسحاق وغيره: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم جلد في الإفك رجلين وامرأة: مسطحا وحسان وحمنة، وذكره الترمذي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri quotes Ibn ʿAbbas saying the Messenger flogged Ibn Ubayy eighty lashes and that he has the Fire as punishment in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: وذكر القشيري عن ابن عباس قال: جلد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ابن أبي ثمانين جلدة، وله في الآخرة عذاب النار

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri says the established reports name Ibn Ubayy, Hassan, and Hamna as flogged; Mistah’s explicit accusation is unproven, though he heard and spread the talk.
rows.anchor: والذي ثبت في الأخبار أنه ضرب ابن أبي وضرب حسان وحمنة، وأما مسطح فلم يثبت عنه قذف صريح

rows.speaker: الماوردي وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi and others report disagreement over whether the Prophet applied the prescribed punishment to the slanderers.
rows.anchor: اختلفوا هل حد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أصحاب الإفك على قولين

rows.speaker: الماوردي وغيره
rows.claim: One view says he punished none: legal penalties require confession or evidence, and divine disclosure alone did not oblige him to impose them, just as it did not oblige him to kill hypocrites despite knowing their unbelief.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أنه لم يحد أحدا من أصحاب الإفك لأن الحدود إنما تقام بإقرار أو ببينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi rejects the no-punishment view as false and contrary to the explicit Qur’anic command to flog accusers who fail to produce four witnesses.
rows.anchor: قلت: وهذا فاسد مخالف لنص القرآن

rows.speaker: الماوردي وغيره
rows.claim: The second view says the Prophet imposed the hadd on ʿAbd Allah b. Ubayy, Mistah b. Uthatha, Hassan b. Thabit, and Hamna bint Jahsh.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم حد أهل الإفك عبد الله بن أبي ومسطح بن أثاثة وحسان بن ثابت وحمنة بنت جحش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The steps of Satan are his paths and ways; believers must not follow the route he invites them to take.
rows.anchor: يعني مسالكه ومذاهبه المعنى: لا تسلكوا الطريق الذي يدعوكم إليها الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A khutwa is the distance between two feet; khutwa with fatḥa is the verbal noun of stepping, and its plural is khutuwāt. The text also explains takhaṭṭā as crossing over to someone and cites a Friday-row crossing report.
rows.anchor: وواحد الخطوات خطوة، وهو ما بين القدمين. والخطوة بالفتح المصدر يقال: خطوت خطوة، وجمعها خطوات

rows.speaker: الجمهور وعاصم والأعمش
rows.claim: The majority read khutuwāt with the ṭāʾ vowelled u; ʿAsim and al-Aʿmash read it with the ṭāʾ quiescent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «خطوات» بضم الطاء. وسكنها عاصم والأعمش

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read zakā with an ungeminated kāf, meaning that none would be guided, accept Islam, or recognize right guidance.
rows.anchor: بتخفيف الكاف أي ما اهتدى ولا أسلم ولا عرف رشدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative meaning of zakā is to become sound or righteous, from zakā yazkū zakāʾ.
rows.anchor: أي ما صلح يقال: زكا يزكو زكاء أي صلح

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو حيوة
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read the verb with a geminated kāf: God alone purifies, guides, and cleanses people by His favor, not through their deeds.
rows.anchor: وشددها الحسن وأبو حيوة أي أن تزكيته لكم وتطهيره وهدايته إنما هي بفضله لا بأعمالكم

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi treats the prohibition against following Satan as parenthetical; “none of you would ever be purified” answers both that clause and the preceding “were it not for God’s favor.”
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: { يأيها الذين آمنوا لا تتبعوا خطوات الشيطان }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The well-known account says this verse was revealed about Abu Bakr and Mistah, his poor maternal cousin and a poor Badr veteran among the Emigrants; Mistah b. Uthatha b. ʿAbbad b. al-Muttalib b. ʿAbd Manaf was reportedly named ʿAwf, with Mistah as his sobriquet.
rows.anchor: المشهور من الروايات أن هذه الآية نزلت في قصة أبي بكر بن أبي قحافة رضي الله عنه ومسطح بن أثاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Bakr supported Mistah because of poverty and kinship, then swore to stop after the slander. Mistah apologized that he attended Hassan’s gatherings only to hear, not speak; Abu Bakr said he had laughed and joined in, and the verse was revealed after Abu Bakr maintained his oath.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو بكر رضي الله عنه ينفق عليه لمسكنته وقرابته فلما وقع أمر الإفك وقال فيه مسطح ما قال، حلف أبو بكر ألا ينفق عليه

rows.speaker: الضحاك وابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and Ibn ʿAbbas say a group of believers cut off their support from everyone who spoke about ʿAʾisha, and the verse was revealed concerning all of them.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك وابن عباس: إن جماعة من المؤمنين قطعوا منافعهم عن كل من قال في الإفك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi says the first account is more sound, while the verse applies to the whole community through the end of time: a person of means must not swear off helping someone of this kind forever.
rows.anchor: والأول أصح غير أن الآية تتناول الأمة إلى يوم القيامة بألا يغتاظ ذو فضل وسعة فيحلف ألا ينفع من هذه صفته غابر الدهر

words: أَلَا تُحِبُّونَ أَن يَغْفِرَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ
rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: A sound report says that after the ten verses beginning “those who brought the slander are a group among you” were revealed, Abu Bakr swore to stop supporting Mistah; following the revelation through “do you not love that God forgive you,” he said he wanted God’s forgiveness and restored the allowance permanently. Ibn al-Mubarak called this the Qur’an’s most hopeful verse.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر وكان ينفق على مسطح لقرابته وفقره: والله لا أنفق عليه شيئا أبدا بعد الذي قال لعائشة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shows that slander, though a grave sin, does not erase deeds: God still describes Mistah with faith and migration; major sins likewise do not annul works, whereas associating partners with God does.
rows.anchor: في هذه الآية دليل على أن القذف وإن كان كبيرا لا يحبط الأعمال لأن الله تعالى وصف مسطحا بعد قوله بالهجرة والإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial bāʾ in buyūt is read with either ḍamma or kasra.
rows.anchor: الباء في «بيوت» تضم وتكسر وقد تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some attach “in houses” to “lamp” in the preceding light verse; others attach it to “he is glorified therein,” in which case one pauses at “Knowing.”
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا التأويل يوقف على «عليم»

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari reports Abu al-ʿAbbas’s view that the phrase is circumstantial for the lamp, glass, and star, as if saying that they are in houses.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: سمعت أبا العباس يقول هو حال للمصباح والزجاجة والكوكب كأنه قال وهي في بيوت

rows.speaker: الترمذي الحكيم محمد بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Muhammad b. ʿAli treats “in houses” as a separate statement that God is in the houses; he cites a report that one who sits in a mosque is in the company of his Lord and a Torah report describing God’s welcome and Paradise as the believer’s hospitality when visiting the mosque.
rows.anchor: منفصل، كأنه يقول: الله في بيوت أذن الله أن ترفع

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says that attaching the phrase to “he is glorified therein,” or making it govern “men,” permits pausing at “God knows everything.”
rows.anchor: حسن الوقف على قوله «والله بكل شيء عليم»

rows.speaker: الرماني
rows.claim: Al-Rummani attaches the phrase to “is kindled,” which means there is no pause at “Knowing.”
rows.anchor: هي متعلقة ب«يوقد» وعليه فلا يوقف على «عليم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To explain a singular lamp and niche with plural houses, one answer is a shifting address that begins in the singular and ends in the plural, as at 65:1; another is that each individual house is intended; a third compares it to the moon placed “in them” at 71:16 though it is in only one of them.
rows.anchor: هذا من الخطاب المتلون الذي يفتح بالتوحيد ويختم بالجمع كقوله تعالى: يأيها النبي إذا طلقتم النسآء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والحسن
rows.claim: The first of five views identifies the houses as mosques set apart for worship, whose light shines for heaven’s people as stars shine for earth’s people.
rows.anchor: الأول: أنها المساجد المخصوصة لله تعالى بالعبادة، وأنها تضيء لأهل السماء كما تضيء النجوم لأهل الأرض قاله ابن عباس ومجاهد والحسن

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A second view attributed to al-Hasan identifies the houses as those of Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: الثاني: هي بيوت بيت المقدس عن الحسن أيضا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: A third view attributed to Mujahid identifies the houses as the Prophet’s homes.
rows.anchor: الثالث: بيوت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن مجاهد أيضا

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: A fourth view, from ʿIkrima, identifies them as houses in general.
rows.anchor: الرابع: هي البيوت كلها قاله عكرمة

rows.speaker: ابن بريدة
rows.claim: A fifth view identifies four mosques built only by prophets: the Kaʿba, the house at Jericho, the mosque of Medina, and the mosque of Quba.
rows.anchor: أنها المساجد الأربعة التي لم يبنها إلا نبي: الكعبة وبيت أريحا ومسجد المدينة ومسجد قباء قاله ابن بريدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of glorifying God morning and evening supports the view that the houses are mosques; al-Qurtubi prefers the first view, citing Anas’s report from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: الأظهر القول الأول لما رواه أنس بن مالك عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports the Prophet saying that whoever loves God should love him, his Companions, the Qur’an, and mosques: they are God’s courtyards and buildings, blessed and protected, where worshippers pray and God attends to their needs.
rows.anchor: من أحب الله عز وجل فليحبني ومن أحبني فليحب أصحابي ومن أحب أصحابي فليحب القرآن ومن أحب القرآن فليحب المساجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adhina means God commanded and decreed; its basic sense is knowledge and enabling without prohibition, strengthened when joined to command and execution.
rows.anchor: معناه أمر وقضى. وحقيقة الإذن العلم والتمكين دون حظر

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة
rows.claim: Mujahid and ʿIkrima take “be raised” to mean built and elevated, as in the verse about Abraham raising the foundations of the House.
rows.anchor: قيل: معناه تبنى وتعلى قاله مجاهد وعكرمة. ومنه قوله تعالى: وإذ يرفع إبراهيم القواعد من البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report promises that whoever builds a mosque with his own money will have a house built for him in Paradise; many reports encourage building mosques.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا المعنى أحاديث كثيرة تحض على بنيان المساجد

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Hasan al-Basri and others take “be raised” to mean revered and honored, with mosques’ status elevated and their filth removed.
rows.anchor: يرفع شأنها، وتطهر من الأنجاس والأقذار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report likens a mosque shrinking away from impurity to skin shrinking from fire.
rows.anchor: المسجد لينزوي من النجاسة كما ينزوي الجلد من النار

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Ibn Majah transmits from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri that whoever removes harm from a mosque will have a house built for him in Paradise.
rows.anchor: وروى ابن ماجه في سننه عن أبي سعيد الخدري

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿAʾisha reports that the Prophet ordered mosques to be established in residential areas, cleaned, and perfumed.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عائشة قالت: أمرنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أن نتخذ المساجد في الدور وأن تطهر وتطيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars differ over decorating and carving mosques: some disapprove, while others permit it.
rows.anchor: إن المراد بنيانها فهل تزين وتنقش

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Abu Dawud transmits from Anas that the Hour will not come until people boast about their mosques.
rows.anchor: روى حماد بن سلمة عن أيوب عن أبي قلابة عن أنس وقتادة عن أنس

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari transmits Anas’s statement that people will boast about mosques and then maintain them only a little.
rows.anchor: يتباهون بها ثم لا يعمرونها إلا قليلا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas predicts that people will adorn mosques as Jews and Christians adorned theirs.
rows.anchor: لتزخرفنها كما زخرفت اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: A report in al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim’s Nawadir al-Usul from Abu al-Dardaʾ warns that decorating mosques and adorning Qur’ans will bring ruin.
rows.anchor: من حديث أبي الدرداء قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those permitting decoration argue that it honors mosques, as they understand “be raised” here to mean “be honored.”
rows.anchor: احتج من أباح ذلك بأن فيه تعظيم المساجد

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: It is reported that ʿUthman built the Prophet’s mosque with teak and made it handsome.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عثمان أنه بنى مسجد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالساج وحسنه

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa permits decorating mosques with gold wash.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حنيفة: لا بأس بنقش المساجد بماء الذهب

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAziz is reported to have lavishly decorated and developed the Prophet’s mosque while governor, before becoming caliph, without anyone objecting.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عمر بن عبد العزيز أنه نقش مسجد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وبالغ في عمارته وتزيينه، وذلك في زمن ولايته قبل خلافته، ولم ينكر عليه أحد ذلك

rows.speaker: الوليد بن عبد الملك
rows.claim: Al-Walid b. ʿAbd al-Malik reportedly spent on building and adorning Damascus Mosque three times the revenue of Syria.
rows.anchor: وذكر أن الوليد بن عبد الملك أنفق في عمارة مسجد دمشق وفي تزيينه مثل خراج الشأم ثلاث مرات

rows.speaker: سليمان بن داود
rows.claim: Solomon son of David is reported to have built the Jerusalem mosque with elaborate decoration.
rows.anchor: وروي أن سليمان بن داود عليهما السلام بنى مسجد بيت المقدس وبالغ في تزيينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As part of their veneration, mosques must be protected from foul odors, vile speech, and other such harms.
rows.anchor: ومما تصان عنه المساجد وتنزه عنه الروائح الكريهة والأقوال السيئة وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A sound report from Ibn ʿUmar says that during the Tabuk expedition the Prophet prohibited anyone who had eaten garlic from coming to the mosques.
rows.anchor: وقد صح من حديث ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jabir b. ʿAbd Allah reports the Prophet prohibiting those who ate garlic, onion, or leek from approaching the mosque because angels are harmed by what harms people.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث جابر بن عبد الله عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: In a sermon transmitted by Muslim, ʿUmar says the Prophet treated onion and garlic as foul: when he smelled them from a man in the mosque, he had the man taken to al-Baqiʿ and advised people to cook them thoroughly.
rows.anchor: وقال عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه في خطبته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By analogy, anyone who harms mosque neighbors through abusive speech, an offensive odor, or an injurious illness such as leprosy may be removed while the harm persists; the same restriction applies to public prayer, study, and banquet gatherings, including pungent foods.
rows.anchor: وإذا كانت العلة في إخراجه من المسجد أنه يتأذى به ففي القياس أن كل من تأذى به جيرانه في المسجد

rows.speaker: أبو عمر بن عبد البر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr recounts that his teacher Abu ʿUmar Ahmad b. ʿAbd al-Malik b. Hisham ruled that an abusive man whose neighbors complained and agreed about his harm should be excluded from the mosque and congregational prayer while the condition persisted.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمر بن عبد البر: وقد شاهدت شيخنا أبا عمر أحمد بن عبد الملك بن هشام رحمه الله أفتى

rows.speaker: أبو عمر أحمد بن عبد الملك بن هشام
rows.claim: The teacher justified excluding the abusive man by analogy to the garlic report, saying his harm exceeded that of eating garlic; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr adds that disconnected reports say lies make angels retreat because of their stench, so known liars may also be excluded.
rows.anchor: فاستدل بحديث الثوم، وقال: هو عندي أكثر أذى من أكل الثوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi cites disconnected reports that an angel withdraws from a person who tells a lie because of its foul odor.
rows.anchor: وفي الآثار المرسلة «أن الرجل ليكذب الكذبة فيتباعد عنه الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars hold that the prohibition applies to all mosques; some restrict it to the Prophet’s mosque because Gabriel descended there and a report says “our mosque.” Al-Qurtubi prefers the general rule since mosque status is the stated legal cause.
rows.anchor: والأول أصح، لأنه ذكر الصفة في الحكم وهي المسجدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabi transmits from Anas a report depicting the world’s mosques as adorned white mounts at Judgment Day, led by their callers to prayer and imams and accompanied by their regular worshippers, who pass like lightning and are identified as the mosque-going, prayer-keeping community of Muhammad.
rows.anchor: يأتي الله يوم القيامة بمساجد الدنيا كأنها نجائب بيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general promise that only believers maintain God’s mosques supports applying the ruling to every mosque.
rows.anchor: وفي التنزيل إنما يعمر مساجد الله من آمن بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says that seeing a man regularly attend the mosque is grounds to testify to his faith, citing 9:18.
rows.anchor: وقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: " إذا رأيتم الرجل يعتاد المسجد فاشهدوا له بالإيمان إن الله تعالى يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mosques are also to be protected from buying, selling, and other distractions.
rows.anchor: السادسة: وتصان المساجد أيضا عن البيع والشراء وجميع الاشتغال

rows.speaker: سليمان بن بريدة عن أبيه
rows.claim: Muslim reports that, after a man called out asking who would find a red camel, the Prophet replied, “May you not find it; mosques were built for their purpose.”
rows.anchor: أخرجه مسلم من حديث سليمان بن بريدة عن أبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s response establishes prayer, remembrance, and Qur’an recitation as the normal mosque activities.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أن الأصل ألا يعمل في المسجد غير الصلوات والأذكار وقراءة القرآن

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports in Muslim that a Bedouin urinated in the mosque; the Prophet stopped people from interrupting him, explained that mosques are for remembrance, prayer, and Qur’an, and ordered water poured over the place.
rows.anchor: وكذا جاء مفسرا من حديث أنس قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command that God’s name be mentioned in mosques from the verse supports reserving them for worship and remembrance.
rows.anchor: خرجه مسلم. ومما يدل على هذا من الكتاب

rows.speaker: معاوية بن الحكم السلمي
rows.claim: Muslim transmits the Prophet telling Muʿawiya b. al-Hakam al-Sulami that mosques are not for ordinary human conversation, but for glorification, magnification, and Qur’an recitation.
rows.anchor: وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم لمعاوية بن الحكم السلمي

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar rebuked a man for making noise in the mosque, asking whether he knew where he was.
rows.anchor: وسمع عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه صوت رجل في المسجد

rows.speaker: خلف بن أيوب
rows.claim: Khalaf b. Ayyub left the mosque to answer his servant’s worldly question, explaining that he had avoided worldly talk there for a long time and disliked breaking that practice.
rows.anchor: فقيل له في ذلك فقال: ما تكلمت في المسجد بكلام الدنيا منذ كذا وكذا

rows.speaker: عمرو بن شعيب
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhi transmits from ʿAmr b. Shuʿayb, from his father and grandfather, that the Prophet forbade reciting poetry in the mosque, buying and selling, and gathering before Friday prayer; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan, and al-Bukhari, Ishaq, and others used it as evidence.
rows.anchor: روى الترمذي من حديث عمرو بن شعيب عن أبيه عن جده

rows.speaker: أحمد وإسحاق
rows.claim: Some scholars disapprove of buying and selling in the mosque; Ahmad and Ishaq hold this view.
rows.anchor: وقد كره قوم من أهل العلم البيع والشراء في المسجد وبه يقول أحمد وإسحاق

rows.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
rows.claim: A report says Jesus found people trading in a mosque, chased them with his cloak, and called them sons of vipers for turning God’s mosques into markets, saying this was the market of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: وروي أن عيسى ابن مريم عليهما السلام أتى على قوم يتبايعون في المسجد

rows.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
rows.claim: Some Shafiʿi colleagues disliked teaching children in mosques if it was paid, treating it as a kind of sale; even unpaid instruction was opposed because children may leave dirt and soil the mosque.
rows.anchor: وقد كره بعض أصحابنا تعليم الصبيان في المساجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic instruction quoted here says to keep children and the insane from mosques, along with swords, legal punishments, raised voices, and disputes, and to perfume mosques on Fridays and place water vessels at their doors.
rows.anchor: وقد أمر صلى الله عليه وسلم بتنظيفها وتطييبها فقال
